pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 150: Listening: for about an hour. (Gherkin's fastest ever.)*

The frost was thick enough to squeak. I had been awake for four hours, staring at the ceiling, counting the tiles in the bathroom. I could not sleep. The silence in the flat was too loud, so I grabbed my torch and my denim jacket and went down the stairs. Ninety-two steps. I counted them all.

The garden was a held breath. The air was sharp and cold, and the glass of the Winter Room was white with ice. I walked to the Spring Room, where the bench usually sat. It was empty, except for Gherkin.

He was awake. His mossy shell caught the beam of my torch. He did not move. He did not blink. I stood there, holding the light, and waited. One minute passed. Then two. I checked my watch. I have never once in my life been so happy to be doing nothing.

"Good evening," I whispered.

He turned his head. It was a slow, deliberate rotation, like a camera panning across a view.

"I want to tell you a story," he said.

I looked at my watch. It was four minutes later. I put the watch away.
pages.image: A thin girl with round glasses and a denim jacket stands in a dark, frosted garden holding a flashlight, illuminating a small, mossy tortoise on a stone bench; the background is a walled garden with glass-roofed rooms under a starry night sky.

pages.text:
"Three hundred years ago," Gherkin said, "there was a boy. He was much like you. Thin. Impatient. He planted an apple pip in this spot." He tapped the ground with a claw. "It was a good pip. From a good tree."

The boy dug it up every morning. Once, then twice, then every hour. He wanted to see the root. He wanted to know if it was working.

"It died," Gherkin said. The voice was flat. Not sad. Just a fact.

The boy was so sorry he planted another one. But this time, he did not dig it up. He sat beside it. He sat there in the sun, and in the rain, and in the cold. He did nothing. For one whole year, he did absolutely nothing but wait.

The tree grew. It grew tall and strong, and it dropped apples that were sweet and heavy. The boy grew old beside it, and his hair turned white, and his hands got rough, but he never once rushed it again.
pages.image: A young man in old-fashioned clothes sits on a stone bench in a sunny garden, resting his chin on his hands while looking at a small sapling in the ground, with a large tortoise watching from the grass nearby.

pages.text:
"That boy," Gherkin said, "had a very long life. And he never once hurried it."

I looked at the tortoise. "You were here?"

"I was his tortoise. I was already old when he was born."

He turned his head again, very slowly, to look at the glass roof above us. The stars were coming out, one by one, through the thin ice.

"When he died, the garden asked me to stay. I have been waiting since then. For someone to tell the truth in it. And to mean it. Most people talk. They shout. They lie about how much they love things. But they do not mean it."

He looked at me. His eyes were dark and deep and still.

"I am waiting for a true word," he said. "Not a loud one. Just a true one."
pages.image: Gherkin, a hat-sized old tortoise with a mossy shell, looks up at a starry night sky through a glass roof, while Sana stands nearby holding a small flashlight whose beam lights his face

pages.text:
I sat down on the bench, the stone cold through my jeans, and asked if he minded being slow, or being stuck here watching things grow.

Gherkin did not answer immediately. The silence stretched out until it felt like a held breath, and the familiar itch to fill it began to burn in my chest. I wanted to check my watch, or say something else, or move my legs, but I forced my hands to stay still in my lap and I waited.

"Mm," he said at last. The sound was small, barely louder than the wind in the glass.

"I mind the world's being fast," he said. "Not myself."

He turned his head to look at me, his eyes dark and deep.

"It is not that you are slow, Sana. It is that you keep leaving before it grows."

I opened my mouth because I had so many things to say, a whole list of reasons about why I was impatient, why I checked the bean every hour, and why I counted the ninety-two steps up to our flat. I wanted to argue, to explain, to prove that I was trying, but the words felt heavy in my throat, like a mouthful of dry bread that would not go down.
pages.image: A girl in a denim jacket sits on a cold stone bench in a dark garden, listening intently to a small tortoise; the background is a walled garden with glass-roofed rooms under a starry night sky.

pages.text:
The cold moved into my legs as I leaned back, watching stars that held still like a paused video. I did not mean to sleep. I only wanted one more minute of quiet. Then my eyelids got heavy, like wet biscuits.

When I woke, the light was pale blue. The torch lay on the ground, its beam making a cone of dust. My jacket was draped over Gherkin’s shell. He had not moved. He had not taken it off.

I sat up. My neck cracked, a sound like stepping on a crisp. The bench was humming. It was a low vibration, deeper than a purr, and the stone was warm under my hand.

Beside my fingers, in a crack in the paving, a single white flower had opened. It was a snowdrop. That is not a plant that lives here. It is not a plant that lives in winter. But it was there, quiet and white and true.
